chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
title: Earl Hines on the radio and listening in Texas
summary: In 1928-29 Texas musicians listened on the radio to Earl Hines, Herman Waldman and Alphonso Trent.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well, one thing I was going to say to you: I take it in those days that Earl and Chicago, because of radio, was probably a fairly big influence in Kansas City, wasn't it?
Well, don't forget now, Earl was the influence on us in Texas.

In 1928 or '29, we used to, all the gang used to make it to that radio. Hear that down-beat (phonetic), "Earl "Father" Hines!" (laughter) "Chant of the Weeds" (phonetic) or not "Chant of the Weeds," but--
"Deep Forest." Man, let me tell you, we'd sit there all night; we heard that "Rosetta" and all that stuff, man. Cat said, "Man, listen at that so-and-so!"
--the radio. You wouldn't know how to get New York on those radios too easily, would you?

Yeah, well it seemed like it was a network. Now you see, in the daytime in Texas, we had a band that'd come from 12 noon to 1, from the Gunter Hotel in San Antonio that was the nearest to nice, soft society swing, you know.
Herman Walder (phonetic) was the name of it. Herman Waldman, m-a-n.

Waldman, and so the guys-- everybody, we were workin' in the daytime, you know, shinin' shoes. Now I did that after I graduated from high school, you know. I worked in a shoeshine parlor in the daytime and worked at nights when I had a gig, you know, with the groups. So at noon all of us would make it to that Chinese restaurant where they had that radio on. We'd hear that band coming from the Gunter Hotel. And then we could get, from time to time, Alphonso Trent (phonetic) coming from that hotel in Dallas--I just called the name of it?
